segments.voice: The memorial is this morning. Zoe has one line to say, and she's afraid she'll freeze reading it off her phone. Inés's grandmother never needed paper: she prayed her rosary by heart, bead by bead. So, yesterday's question. A Persian poet took his very name from that kind of knowing.
screen: `ONE LINE, ONE PHONE.` → `THE ROSARY, BY HEART.` → `A POET NAMED FOR IT.`

segments.voice: His given name was Shams al-Din Muhammad, of Shiraz. The name we know him by is a title. In Muslim communities, a hafiz is someone who has memorized the whole Quran, and the title is an honor. Tradition says he earned it, and his own Divan seems to agree. In one couplet he talks to himself: I've seen nothing sweeter than your poetry, Hafiz, by the Quran you keep in your breast. He swears by the book he carries inside. That's the teaching under the name. In Islam, keeping the Quran by heart isn't a party trick. It means the words go where you go, into the dark, into old age, into a room with no book in it. Inés's grandmother had the same kind of treasure: the rosary's prayers, worn smooth by years of saying. For today, one thing. What you hold by heart is there when the paper isn't.

segments.voice: Choose one line you love: from your own tradition, from this week, or your own four lines. Say it out loud, then again without looking, and again, until it stays. Let the last minute be the line, said quietly, by heart.
